title: A Green Light With Guardrails: How Smart Leaders Approve Risky Ideas
documentTitle: Email from Eileen Naughton to Google Employees re: Google Ad Exchange Product GPS Presentation (May 19, 2008)
excerptForBlog: Forwarding you the final Ad Exchange deck that Neal Mohan and Scott Spencer presented at the GPS Friday afternoon. Larry and Susan attended. Larry gave a cautionary green light to proceed on developing the business case. He did not 100% agree to a fully open network — suggested Google set some baseline controls about which exchanges to let in, competitors to restrict, and operating policy. But in the end it was a green light to develop the business case.

lessonTitle: A Green Light With Guardrails: How Smart Leaders Approve Risky Ideas
pullQuote: The most valuable approval you can get isn't a blank check — it's a conditional yes that tells you exactly where the limits are.
leadershipTraits: Thinks in competitive exposure, not just product potential
Precise about what is and isn't decided
Protects access as a strategic asset
situation: On May 19, 2008, Eileen Naughton forwarded an internal summary of a Google Ad Exchange strategy presentation to colleagues. The presenters were Neal Mohan and Scott Spencer. Larry Page and Susan Wojcicki attended. The question on the table: should Google open its ad exchange to outside competitors and third-party networks?
insight: Larry Page approved moving forward — but not fully. The email records that he 'gave a cautionary green light to proceed on developing the business case' while explicitly flagging that he did 'not 100% agree to a fully open network.' He proposed that Google 'set some baseline controls about which exchanges to let in, competitors to restrict, and operating policy.' This is a classic **platform governance** move. Google was weighing the benefits of openness — more liquidity, more advertisers, a bigger market — against the risk of empowering rivals on its own infrastructure. A fully open network could hand competitors a free ride. By asking for baseline controls, Page was separating two decisions: whether to build the business case at all (yes) and how open to make the network (not decided yet). That sequencing is disciplined. It avoids committing to a structure before the economics are understood.
application: When your team brings a big strategic proposal, resist the pressure to approve it all at once. Give a conditional green light: authorize the business case, but name the specific constraint you're not ready to drop — a pricing floor, a partner type you won't let in, a capability you won't share. Write it down in one sentence, the way this email does. It keeps momentum alive while preserving the decision you haven't made yet.
